module_title: Daily Care and Management of Adult Birds

lessons.title: Routine Morning and Evening Checks for Guinea Fowl and Quail
lessons.body: Start your day with the birds before they start theirs. At first light, walk to the pens quietly. Count every bird. For guinea fowl, a flock of 20 should all be present; for quail, a cage of 30 should show no empty spaces. Look for any bird sitting apart, panting, or with drooping wings. Check water first: a guinea fowl drinks about 250 ml per day, a quail about 50 ml. In hot weather, refill waterers twice daily. Ensure water is clean and coolânot hot from the sun. Next, check feed troughs. Adult guinea fowl eat 80â100 g of feed per day; quail eat 25â30 g. Remove any wet or mouldy feed immediately. Look at droppings: healthy droppings are firm and grey-green with a white cap. Watery or bloody droppings mean sicknessâisolate that bird. In the evening, before sunset, do a second check. Count birds again. Guinea fowl may roost in trees if free-ranging; ensure they come back to the pen. Quail are ground birds; they should be inside the cage. Collect eggs: guinea fowl eggs are thick-shelled and often hidden in grass; quail eggs are small and may fall through wire floors if not collected promptly. Check for predators: snakes, rats, and hawks are common. Repair any holes in netting. Lock doors. Note any unusual behaviour in a notebook. This routine takes 15 minutes morning and evening but prevents most losses. Consistency is keyâbirds thrive on predictability.

lessons.title: Cleaning and Disinfecting Cages and Pens
lessons.body: Dirty cages cause disease. Clean weekly, disinfect monthly, and do a deep clean every three months. For quail cages, remove birds to a holding box. Scrape droppings with a putty knife or flat stick. Use a wire brush to scrub perches and corners. Mix 1 part bleach to 10 parts water (or use 2 tablespoons of washing soda per litre of hot water). Scrub all surfaces. Rinse thoroughly with clean waterâbleach residue can burn birdsâ feet. Let dry in the sun; sunlight kills many germs. For guinea fowl pens, remove old bedding (wood shavings, straw, or sand). Replace with fresh, dry material. Sprinkle agricultural lime on the floor to reduce ammonia smell and kill parasites. If using sand, sieve it and sun-dry. Disinfect feeders and waterers daily by washing with soap and rinsing. Once a week, soak them in disinfectant for 10 minutes. For free-range guinea fowl, move their night shelter every few weeks to new ground to avoid parasite build-up. Quail are sensitive to ammonia; if you smell ammonia, clean immediately. Wear gloves and a nose mask when cleaning to protect yourself. After cleaning, wash your hands and change clothes. Keep a cleaning schedule on the wall: Mondayâwaterers, Tuesdayâfeeders, Wednesdayâcage floors, etc. This prevents skipped tasks. Remember: a clean environment reduces stress, respiratory infections, and coccidiosis. Healthy birds grow faster and lay more eggs.

lessons.title: Managing Guinea Fowl Free-Range Behavior Without Losing Birds
lessons.body: Guinea fowl love to roam. They can fly up to 2 metres high and walk 1 kilometre a day. Without management, you will lose birds to predators, cars, or theft. Start by training them to a home pen. Keep young guinea fowl confined for the first 6â8 weeks. Feed them inside the pen at the same time each morning and evening. Use a distinctive callâlike shaking a tin of maizeâso they associate that sound with food. After 8 weeks, let them out in the late afternoon for short periods. They will return to roost if the pen is safe and has feed. Always provide a secure night shelter. A simple hut with perches 1.5 metres high works well. Close the door at dusk after all birds are inside. Count them. If any are missing, search nearby treesâthey often roost high. To reduce wandering, plant tall grasses or shrubs around the pen as a visual barrier. Provide a dust bath area inside the pen; guinea fowl use dust to clean feathers and reduce parasites. Keep a dog trained to guard poultry, or use a donkeyâthey chase predators. Never let guinea fowl free-range during planting season; they eat young crops. In areas with hawks, keep birds in a covered run. If you must free-range, do it after 10 a.m. when hawks are less active. Always have a rooster or a few older guinea fowl as leaders; they teach younger ones to come home. Losing birds is costlyâeach guinea fowl is worth money and time. Management is better than replacement.

lessons.title: Stress Reduction: Handling, Noise, and Weather Extremes
lessons.body: Stress kills birds quietly. Guinea fowl and quail are easily frightened. Sudden noise, rough handling, or extreme heat can cause them to stop eating, stop laying, or die. Handle birds only when necessary. To catch a quail, use a small net or cup both hands gently around the body, keeping wings folded. Never grab by the head or legs. For guinea fowl, use a catching hook or a large net. Hold them with both hands supporting the breast and wings. Work quietly and slowly. Keep children and dogs away from pens. Loud noisesâmotorbikes, radios, shoutingâcause panic. Quail may pile up in a corner and suffocate. Place pens away from roads and noisy areas. Provide hiding spots: small boxes, leafy branches, or shade cloth. For heat stress, offer cool water with electrolytes (1 teaspoon of salt and 1 teaspoon of sugar per litre). Misting the roof or providing shallow pans for foot cooling helps. In cold weather, add extra bedding and block drafts. Guinea fowl are hardy but quail are sensitive below 10Â°C. Use a heat lamp for quail chicks, but adults can tolerate 15Â°C if dry. During storms, bring free-range guinea fowl inside early. Play a radio softly at night to mask sudden sounds. Keep a routine: same feeding times, same person. Birds recognise faces. A calm environment means more eggs: a stressed quail stops laying for days. Reduce stress, increase profit.

lessons.title: Record Keeping for Growth, Egg Production, and Feed Consumption
lessons.body: You cannot manage what you do not measure. Keep a simple notebook or a wall chart. Record daily: number of eggs collected (for guinea fowl and quail separately), amount of feed given (in kilograms), and any dead or sick birds. Weigh a sample of 5 birds every two weeks to track growth. For quail, adult weight should be 150â200 g; for guinea fowl, 1.3â1.6 kg. If weights drop, check feed quality or disease. Egg production: a good quail lays 250â300 eggs per year; a guinea fowl lays 80â150. If your quail lay fewer than 20 eggs per 30 birds per day, something is wrongâmaybe feed, light, or stress. Feed conversion ratio (FCR) = feed eaten divided by weight gained or eggs produced. For quail, FCR for eggs should be about 2.5 kg feed per 1 kg eggs. If FCR rises, you are wasting money. Record expenses: feed, medicine, bedding, labour. At the end of each month, calculate profit: (eggs sold + birds sold) minus expenses. Use a simple table with columns: Date, Eggs, Feed (kg), Deaths, Notes. Keep records for at least one year to see seasonal patterns. Share records with your vet if disease occurs. Good records help you get loans or grants. They also show you which pen or breed performs best. Start todayâeven a rough tally is better than none.

lessons.title: Seasonal Care: Preparing for Rainy and Dry Seasons
lessons.body: Africaâs seasons are tough on poultry. In the rainy season, mud and dampness cause disease. In the dry season, heat and dust cause stress. Prepare early. Before rains, check roofs for leaks. Raise pens on a 30 cm platform of stones or bricks to prevent flooding. Use free-draining bedding like sand or wood shavings. Never let water pool inside. Store feed in airtight drums to prevent mould. Mouldy feed causes aflatoxin poisoningâbirds die suddenly. Vaccinate against Newcastle disease before rains, as it spreads in wet conditions. For guinea fowl, provide a covered dry area; they hate getting wet. Quail cages should have a solid roof and plastic sheeting on the windward side. After rains, check for snails and slugsâthey carry gapeworm. Collect eggs quickly; wet eggs spoil. In the dry season, heat is the enemy. Provide shade: trees, shade cloth, or a thatched roof. Give cool water at least three times a day. Add vitamin C (1 g per litre) to water to reduce heat stress. Wet the ground around pens to cool the air. Never overcrowdâreduce stocking by 20% in peak heat. For quail, mist the roof but not the birds. For guinea fowl, let them free-range early morning and late evening only. Watch for signs of heat stroke: panting, wings held out, lying down. Move such birds to a cool, shaded area and give water with electrolytes. In both seasons, keep a emergency fund for extra feed, water, or medicine. Prepare now, lose less later.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Daily Care & Management of Adult Guinea Fowl and Quail

In African smallholder and semi-commercial poultry systems, adult guinea fowl and quail are often kept as complementary enterprises: guinea fowl for meat, eggs, tick control, and security alarm behaviour; quail for rapid egg and meat turnover. The difference between a profitable flock and a loss-making one is rarely the breed â it is the daily routine. This lesson gives you a practical, business-first reference for managing adult birds so that mortality stays low, egg output stays stable, and feed conversion remains economically viable.

Use this module as a field manual. Keep a printed copy in your poultry house, and train every worker on the morning and evening checks before they handle birds alone.

1. Routine Morning and Evening Checks

Do the same checks at the same time every day. Birds and workers both settle into the rhythm, and problems are caught early â when they are cheap to fix.

Morning (06:00â08:00): Enter quietly. Count birds before they scatter. Look for dead birds, blood, diarrhoea, or drooped wings. Refill clean water first, then feed. Collect eggs immediately â quail eggs in particular crack or get eaten if left. Open vents and remove wet litter.

Evening (17:30â18:30): Count again. Guinea fowl must be inside before dark â they will roost in trees if allowed. Refill waterers for the night. Check for predators (snakes, rats, wild cats). Lock the house. Note anything unusual.

2. Cleaning and Disinfecting Cages and Pens

Dirty housing is the single largest driver of mortality in African smallholder flocks. Quail are especially sensitive to ammonia from droppings; guinea fowl tolerate more, but both suffer respiratory disease in wet, soiled bedding.

Daily: remove wet litter and spilled feed. Weekly: scrape perches, scrub drinkers with soap and clean water, sun-dry them. Monthly: full clean-out â remove all litter, wash floors and walls, apply disinfectant, dry completely before re-stocking. Rotate disinfectants to avoid resistance. Wood ash, lime, and sunlight are free, effective tools where commercial disinfectants are expensive.

Table 1: Cleaning schedule and cost of neglect for adult guinea fowl and quail (Africa smallholder context)
Task Frequency Guinea Fowl Quail Business impact if skipped
Litter removal (wet/dirty spots) Daily Moderate Critical Ammonia burns, respiratory disease, 5â15% mortality
Drinker scrubbing + sun-dry Dailyâweekly Critical Critical Water refusal â 20â30% drop in egg production
Full pen wash + disinfect Monthly Important Important Coccidiosis, fowl typhoid outbreaks
Perch and nest box clean Weekly Important Moderate Dirty eggs, lower hatchability, lower market price
Rodent and snake control Continuous Critical Critical Egg and chick losses up to 30%

Source: Compiled from FAO, Poultry Development Review (2013) and ILRI smallholder poultry husbandry guidelines (ilri.org).

3. Managing Guinea Fowl Free-Range Behaviour Without Losing Birds

Guinea fowl are semi-wild. They fly, roam, and roost in trees â which is why many African farmers lose 20â40% of their flock each year. The solution is routine, not force.

Train birds from a young age: feed them at the same spot every morning and evening, and call them with the same sound. Keep them confined for the first 2â3 weeks after purchase or hatch so they imprint on the homestead. Clip one wing of the strongest fliers only if necessary â never both wings, as birds need balance. Provide tall trees or poles inside the compound as safe roosting options so they don't wander. Always close the house at dusk.

4. Stress Reduction: Handling, Noise, and Weather Extremes

Stress costs money: it suppresses laying, weakens immunity, and increases cannibalism. Quail are far more stress-sensitive than guinea fowl â a loud noise or rough handling can stop egg production for 3â7 days.

Handle birds gently with both hands, supporting the body. Never chase birds. Move slowly. Keep children and dogs away from the pen. During heatwaves, provide shade, cool water, and misting. During cold or rainy spells, block draughts, dry the litter, and increase energy in the feed.

â  SAFETY WARNING â DISINFECTANTS AND MEDICATION

Never mix disinfectants (especially bleach with ammonia-based products) â toxic gases can kill you and your birds. Always wear gloves and a nose mask when cleaning pens or applying chemicals. Store all medicines, vaccines, and disinfectants in a locked cabinet away from children, feed, and water. Follow withdrawal periods strictly before selling eggs or meat for human consumption. If you suspect a notifiable disease (e.g., avian influenza), report immediately to your local veterinary officer â do not sell or move birds.

5. Record Keeping for Growth, Egg Production, and Feed Consumption

You cannot manage what you do not measure. Even a simple exercise book gives you the data to make business decisions: when to cull, when to change feed, when to expand.

Table 2: Essential records for a profitable guinea fowl and quail enterprise
Record What to capture Frequency Business use
Mortality log Date, number, age, suspected cause Daily Detect disease early; calculate survival rate
Egg production Number collected, cracked, sold Daily Calculate lay %, spot drops, price eggs correctly
Feed consumption Kg fed per house per day Daily Compute feed conversion ratio (FCR) and cost per egg
Body weight (sample) Weigh 5â10 birds weekly Weekly Track growth, decide slaughter timing
Health treatments Vaccine, drug, dose, withdrawal date Per event Food safety compliance; avoid residue penalties
Sales & expenses Birds, eggs, feed, labour, drugs Weekly Profit and loss; loan applications

Source: Adapted from FAO, Small-scale poultry production (2004), fao.org/3/y5169e/y5169e00.htm and ILRI market-oriented smallholder poultry guides.

6. Seasonal Care: Preparing for Rainy and Dry Seasons

Rainy season: The biggest risks are wet litter, coccidiosis, and flooded pens. Raise the floor on a platform, dig drainage channels, store feed on pallets above ground, and vaccinate before the rains start. Collect eggs more frequently so they don't get muddy.

Dry season: Heat stress and dust are the enemies. Provide deep shade (trees, shade cloth), cool drinking water several times a day, and dust-bathing areas. In the Sahel and northern savannah, heat can push quail mortality above 15% without intervention.

Transition periods: Watch for sudden temperature swings â these trigger respiratory disease in both species. Increase vitamin C and electrolytes in water during stress periods.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Count all birds morning and evening â record any loss immediately.
  • â Provide clean, cool water before feed every morning.
  • â Collect eggs at least twice daily; store in a cool, clean place.
  • â Remove wet litter and spilled feed daily to prevent ammonia and mould.
  • â Close guinea fowl and quail houses before dusk â no exceptions.
  • â Handle birds calmly; keep noise, dogs, and strangers away from pens.
  • â Record mortality, eggs, feed, and sales in your logbook every day.
  • â Inspect for predators, leaks, and draughts weekly; repair immediately.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • FAO â Small-scale poultry production (Y5169E)
  • FAO â Poultry Development Review
  • ILRI â Smallholder Poultry Research
  • WOAH â Avian Influenza (notifiable disease guidance)
  • CABI â Invasive Species & Poultry Pest Information

Business takeaway: A disciplined daily routine is the cheapest input in your poultry enterprise. It reduces mortality, stabilises egg output, and gives you the records you need to price your products, access credit, and scale. Treat every morning and evening check as an investment â not a chore.

quiz.q: What is the approximate daily water intake for an adult guinea fowl?
quiz.explanation: Adult guinea fowl drink about 250 ml per day, while quail drink about 50 ml.

quiz.q: How often should you refill waterers in hot weather?
quiz.explanation: In hot weather, waterers should be refilled at least twice daily to keep water cool and clean.

quiz.q: What do healthy droppings of guinea fowl look like?
options: B) Firm and grey-green with a white cap
quiz.explanation: Healthy droppings are firm, grey-green with a white cap; changes indicate illness.

quiz.q: Why should you count birds in the evening?
options: B) To ensure all are inside and safe from predators
quiz.explanation: Evening count ensures all birds are safely inside before predators become active.

quiz.q: What is the recommended bleach-to-water ratio for disinfecting cages?
options: A) 1 part bleach to 10 parts water
B) 1 part bleach to 2 parts water
C) 1 part bleach to 20 parts water
D) 1 part bleach to 100 parts water
quiz.explanation: A 1:10 bleach solution is effective for killing germs on cage surfaces.

quiz.q: Why should you rinse cages thoroughly after using bleach?
options: B) To remove bleach residue that can burn birdsâ feet
C) To make the cage shiny
quiz.explanation: Bleach residue can irritate or burn birdsâ feet, so thorough rinsing is essential.

quiz.q: How often should you do a deep clean of quail cages?
quiz.explanation: A deep clean every three months removes built-up dirt and parasites.

quiz.q: What does agricultural lime do in a guinea fowl pen?
options: B) Reduces ammonia smell and kills parasites
quiz.explanation: Agricultural lime neutralises ammonia and helps control parasites on the floor.

quiz.q: Why should you wear a nose mask when cleaning cages?
options: B) To avoid breathing in dust and ammonia
quiz.explanation: Dust and ammonia can harm your lungs; a mask protects your health.

quiz.q: How long should young guinea fowl be confined before free-ranging?
quiz.explanation: Confining for 6â8 weeks helps them imprint on the home pen and reduces wandering.

quiz.q: What sound can be used to train guinea fowl to return to the pen?
options: B) Shaking a tin of maize
quiz.explanation: A distinctive sound like shaking a tin of maize associates with feeding time.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid free-ranging guinea fowl during planting season?
quiz.explanation: Guinea fowl will eat young crops, causing damage to farms.

quiz.q: What is a good way to reduce hawk attacks on free-range guinea fowl?
options: A) Let them out early morning
B) Let them out after 10 a.m.
C) Keep them in a covered run
quiz.explanation: Hawks are less active after 10 a.m., and a covered run provides protection.

quiz.q: How do you safely catch a quail?
options: B) Use a small net or cup both hands gently
C) Chase it into a corner
D) Pick up by one wing
quiz.explanation: Using a net or cupping hands gently avoids injury to the bird.

quiz.q: What is a sign of heat stress in quail?
options: B) Panting and holding wings out
quiz.explanation: Panting and wing spreading are common signs of heat stress.

quiz.q: What simple electrolyte solution can help birds under stress?
options: A) 1 teaspoon salt and 1 teaspoon sugar per litre
quiz.explanation: A salt-sugar solution helps restore electrolytes lost during stress.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep a routine with birds?
options: B) It reduces stress and improves production
C) It makes them grow faster
D) It prevents them from flying away
quiz.explanation: Predictable routines reduce stress, which leads to better health and egg production.

quiz.q: What is the average annual egg production for a good quail?
quiz.explanation: A healthy quail can lay 250â300 eggs per year under good management.

quiz.q: What does FCR stand for in poultry records?
quiz.explanation: FCR measures how efficiently feed is converted into body weight or eggs.

quiz.q: Why should you record daily egg production?
options: B) To monitor health and productivity
quiz.explanation: Daily records help detect drops in production that may indicate disease or stress.

quiz.q: What is a simple way to track growth?
options: A) Weigh a sample of 5 birds every two weeks
quiz.explanation: Weighing a sample provides objective data on growth trends.

quiz.q: Why keep records for at least one year?
quiz.explanation: A full year of records reveals seasonal changes in production and costs.

quiz.q: What should you do before the rainy season to prevent flooding?
options: A) Raise pens on a platform
quiz.explanation: Raising pens on a 30 cm platform keeps them dry during floods.

quiz.q: Why is mouldy feed dangerous?
quiz.explanation: Mouldy feed can contain aflatoxins, which are deadly to poultry.

quiz.q: How can you reduce heat stress in the dry season?
options: A) Provide shade and cool water
quiz.explanation: Shade and cool water help birds regulate body temperature.

quiz.q: What is a sign of heat stroke in guinea fowl?
quiz.explanation: Lying down and panting are signs of heat stroke; move bird to a cool area.

quiz.q: Why should you reduce stocking density in peak heat?
options: A) To give birds more space to cool down
quiz.explanation: Lower density reduces competition for cool spots and airflow.

quiz.q: What should you do with wet eggs collected during rains?
options: B) Dry them quickly and use soon
quiz.explanation: Wet eggs spoil quickly; dry them and use promptly to avoid waste.

quiz.q: Why is it important to check for snails after rains?
quiz.explanation: Snails can carry gapeworm, a parasite that infects poultry.

quiz.q: What is a good emergency preparation for both seasons?
quiz.explanation: An emergency fund helps you buy extra feed, water, or medicine when needed.
